newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Trade, investment to dominate Japan-EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Trade, investment to dominate Japan-EU summit.

text.p: A trade imbalance and disagreements over market access are likely to figure strongly when Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto meets the European Union's presidency for the annual Japan-EU summit in the Hague on Wednesday.

But with relations between the EU and Japan currently as good as they've ever been, officials from both sides expect the meeting to concentrate on strengthening ties rather than on disagreements that do exist.
"Sure there is a trade imbalance and sure, we feel Japan could do a lot more on market access, but it would be wrong to characterise these issues as 'storm clouds'," said one EU official.
"I would say those issues are more likely to be a light summer shower," he said.
Nevertheless, EU officials are likely to want to press Hashimoto to expand on his comments made on Monday regarding Tokyo's huge holdings in U.S. treasuries which sent financial markets into a spin.

Hashimoto said in the past Japan had been tempted to sell some of its treasuries but had not done so. "I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation ... and switch to gold," he said.

While other Japanese officials on Tuesday sought to play down his comments, some analysts have read his message as a thinly-veiled warning to Washington not to press Tokyo too hard over its trade surplus.
The EU, also on the wrong end of a trade imbalance with Japan, would inevitably suffer too if Tokyo did sell some U.S. bills.

Depression on the U.S. bond market would likely spread to Europe and to Europe's bourses, causing market nervousness at a time when most EU governments are grappling to meet conditions for economic and monetary union (EMU).

EU officials will take the opportunity on Wednesday to brief Hashimoto on the EMU situation as Japanese businessmen and analysts -- who have largely ignored the subject -- begin showing more interest.

"EMU is not the sole criterion for deciding where to invest in Europe," said a senior Japanese diplomat. "Flexibility in the labour market is probably the most important criterion, but so too are language, schools and golf courses ...".
Nevertheless, there are some Japanese business people who believe that a single currency is likely to cause some problems for trade.
"In Japan there is a growing interest in EMU. There is no debate -- we believe that is for the Europeans -- but there is interest in the subject," the diplomat said.

"The question is, who will speak for the Euro? If there is an international currency crisis and we need to call someone in the middle of the night, who do we speak to? Mr de Silguy (European monetary commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy). The Germans? The French?"

Other subjects to be discussed during the summit include the EU's recent membership of the Korean Energy Development Organisation, the group set up to press North Korea to focus its nuclear aspirations on energy and not weapons.
They will also discuss global environmental issues, the international fight against drug trafficking and terrorism and African development.
